name: Pedro Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does your working day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead a crew building timber ramps and stair landings on new building sites. My trade certificate and years of work make me one of the people others call when a landing is out of level. I use AI every day to compare drawings and quantities, then measure the built doorway myself. My partner and I have grown children and a few months of expenses saved; I earn about the usual rate and hope to retire from regular site work at sixty-six in 2034 if our income supports it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the AI list is useful for board counts, but the ramp has to work for a person using it. An AI ramp drawing cannot feel the lip that catches a wheelchair at a building doorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead wage to continue. We have one to six months saved and some other construction jobs nearby, though the age-sixty-six retirement target needs a real budget check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading ramp work and use the drawing comparison I already use daily. I would roll a test chair across the finished threshold where site rules allow, and review our future income with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my current job. The small office saving does not change the physical accessibility check or our planned retirement age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check at that threshold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The height of the lip and whether the chair can cross it without a bump. I also check the slope and handrail against the site specification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call today’s AI use new training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It is my ordinary list check. I would only call it learning if I practised a new control or task.

say: I would **use** AI for ramp quantities and physically test the finished threshold.
I would **tell** the crew accessibility is measured by the person using the ramp.
think: My **lead** role looks secure, while retirement still needs income figures.
**Several** months saved and some nearby jobs reduce pressure from a small change.
do: **Keep** leading ramp construction and testing built doorway thresholds.
**Check** age-sixty-six retirement income against household costs with partner.
feel: **Calm** about paid work and familiar daily AI use.
S0.quote: An AI ramp drawing cannot feel the lip that catches a wheelchair at a building doorway.
fieldNote: **Pedro** uses AI every day for drawings but tests the built ramp with a physical accessibility check.
His **high** standing, typical pay and moderate cushion support calm, with retirement still conditional.

steps.text: Keep leading and testing building-site ramp work
Check age-sixty-six retirement budget before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say quicker planning should get timber to site before the ramp crew starts. I would learn the new AI delivery control early and bring the results to our union site meeting so nobody loses paid testing time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry management might count the faster order as a reason to compress our paid fit and access checks. My own hours could fall, and a few months saved would not make that harmless before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practice the new delivery control on a completed ramp and test it on two live jobs. I would keep paid shifts, record threshold-test time and ask the union representative to seek written paid access checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible lost hours but keen to test the tool. A faster AI ramp order is no saving if the person checking wheelchair access loses a paid hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your test of the control show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the right boards and fixings arrived before the paid crew began. I would match the software record to two delivery tickets and the built doorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union representative to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time for a person to check slope, lip and handrail before sign-off. I would bring the time records to the site meeting.

say: I would **learn** new AI delivery controls and test real ramp orders.
I would **bring** paid accessibility checks to the union site meeting.
think: A **compressed** schedule could cut my own hours before retirement.
**Several** months saved give some room but not a reason to accept unpaid checks.
do: **Practice** new AI delivery controls on completed and live ramp jobs.
**Keep** paid ramp shifts and record threshold-check time.
**Seek** union clause paying for slope, lip and handrail checks.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour loss, with tools to act.
S1.quote: A faster AI ramp order is no saving if the person checking wheelchair access loses a paid hour.
fieldNote: His **new** AI practice and concrete union meeting action fit adaptive and progressive traits.
The **risk** is his own paid checking time, which makes anxiety credible despite a few months saved.

steps.text: Learn new AI delivery control on real ramp orders
Keep paid ramp fitting while logging access checks
Seek union clause for paid ramp-access testing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches ramp plans in 2028 when I am sixty, with hands-on robots around 2031 when I am sixty-three. A robot-built ramp in 2031 still needs a paid person to test the slope before a wheelchair reaches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think standard ramp fitting hours could shrink once robots do the cutting and fixing. We have only several months saved, and the few nearby alternatives cannot be assumed to pay for three lost years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a supervised paid trial checking robot-built ramp slopes and handrails, with authority to stop an unsafe opening; a request is not a place on the trial. If hours fall after 2031, I would apply to posted local access-repair jobs only at a wage covering our bills and with written safety authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real wage gap, though I can test and search. I would not leave work at sixty-three unless verified household income covered all the years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop a ramp opening in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slope outside the site specification or a loose rail at the doorway. I would require a paid human check before anyone uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your savings pay for three years out of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A few months saved are a buffer, not three years of wages or guaranteed retirement income.

say: **Thinking** AI changes plans in 2028; robots may fit ramps around 2031.
I would **request**, not assume, a paid supervised access trial.
think: **Three** years of expected wages are exposed before my age-sixty-six target.
A **local** repair move requires a posted role, adequate wage and written safety authority.
do: **Request** paid supervised robot-ramp access trial with stop-opening authority.
**Keep** paid ramp shifts while seeking offered trial place.
**Apply** after hour cuts to posted local access-repair role with adequate pay and safety authority.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour loss, with conditional options.
S2.quote: A robot-built ramp in 2031 still needs a paid person to test the slope before a wheelchair reaches it.
fieldNote: His **trial** remains a request until the builder offers a paid supervised place.
He **requires** a posted local role with household-covering wages and safety authority before applying after lost hours.

steps.text: Keep paid ramp shifts while requesting supervised paid robot trial
Apply after cuts to posted local access-repair job with adequate pay and stop-work authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, and hands-on ramp robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. The physical date meets the retirement age I already hoped for, if our income covers the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could stay in accessibility inspection if retirement is not affordable, but that needs a formal credential and a real posted job. An access-inspection certificate has no value if I cannot stop a ramp with the wrong slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading paid ramp work and review our age-sixty-six budget with my partner. If income falls short and a posted local access-inspector role offers household-covering pay and written stop-opening authority, I would complete a fully funded course on paid time and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the budget rather than certain of a job loss. The years give me time to match training to an actual safe paid vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach beyond ramp fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Formal access inspection and sign-off rules for another crew’s work. I already fit ramps, but an inspector needs documented authority to reject unsafe slopes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is funded but the days are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on paid ramp shifts and look for a paid-time course tied to a posted local role. Our savings are not a training wage.

say: **Robots** around 2034 reach ramp fitting at my original age-sixty-six target.
I would **train** for formal access inspection only if income requires continued work.
think: A **credential** needs a posted safe local role and wages that cover our bills.
**Fully** funded training must also pay the study days.
do: **Enrol** in funded access-inspection training on paid time if income short and posted local job offers bill-covering pay and written stop-opening authority.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted local inspector job with adequate pay and stop-opening authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until retirement income and later job terms are known.
S3.quote: An access-inspection certificate has no value if I cannot stop a ramp with the wrong slope.
fieldNote: **Actual** course completion and later application are distinct conditional actions.
**Retirement** remains the original target; continued work needs an income shortfall, funded paid training and a real adequate safe local role.

steps.text: Check original age-sixty-six retirement income before deciding
Enrol if shortfall in funded paid-time access-inspection course for posted bill-covering local job with stop-opening authority
Apply after qualifying to posted local inspector role with adequate pay and stop-opening authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight, and capable ramp robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. Both dates follow my original age-sixty-six target in 2034, if our household figures allow me to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not assume I am still fitting ramps at seventy-one. If the budget fails, I would want a posted safe local role paying our bills, and the younger crew should still get paid training and checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid ramp work now and check the retirement budget with my partner. If income covers our costs, I would leave regular site work at the original 2034 target; otherwise I would keep working and apply only to posted local access roles at household-covering wages with written safety authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the figures are real, but hopeful about a longer public discussion of access and work. A decade lets us put paid safety duties into site agreements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What agreement would you still want if you retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A 2039 ramp robot should not open a doorway before a paid worker tests wheelchair access. I would raise it at the union meeting now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise to advise sites in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I may already be retired, and I will not invent a paid role. I would support the younger workers’ safety agreement without claiming a job.

say: The 2036 **thinking** change and 2039 robots may follow my original retirement.
I would **raise** a paid human ramp test at the union meeting now.
think: **Later** paid work depends on the household income falling short.
A **real** local vacancy needs adequate pay and written stop-opening authority.
do: **Retire** at original 2034 target only if verified income covers household costs.
**Seek** a union agreement for paid human ramp tests and stop-opening authority.
**Apply** if still working to posted local access role with adequate pay and written safety authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until retirement figures are verified, hopeful about safer agreements.
S4.quote: A 2039 ramp robot should not open a doorway before a paid worker tests wheelchair access.
fieldNote: His **progressive** concern leads to a real union meeting request for paid access tests.
He does **not** assume employment at seventy-one; later applications need an income shortfall, posted safe local role and adequate wages.

steps.text: Retire at original 2034 target only if verified income covers bills
Seek union agreement for paid human ramp access tests
Apply if working to posted local access role with adequate pay and stop-opening authority

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because robot ramp work could cut three wage years before my planned retirement. An offered paid trial and posted nearby inspection role with household-covering pay and safety authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can stop a ramp with the wrong slope before a wheelchair user reaches it. I like new tools, but the person testing access must be paid and heard. A ramp is finished when someone can use the doorway safely, not when an AI drawing looks complete.

headlineQuote: A ramp is finished when someone can use the doorway safely, not when an AI drawing looks complete.
portrait: **Pedro** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified senior carpenter who leads building-site ramp and landing work.
He **has** typical pay, one to six months saved, a partner, grown children and some nearby jobs.
He **uses** AI daily, learns new controls early and takes concrete union action for paid access checks.
He **hopes** to retire at sixty-six in 2034 if income covers costs; later work requires a budget shortfall.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could cut ramp wages three years before his original age-sixty-six target.
whatWouldHelp: An **offered** paid supervised trial and a posted local inspection job with adequate pay and stop-opening authority would help.
